data:
Some problems are too small to buy a solution for and too annoying to leave alone.
Cue came out of one of those. A handful of displays, a remote that worked until it didn’t, and the kind of stubborn curiosity that turns a Saturday afternoon fix into a weeks-long detour through HDMI-CEC specs, Raspberry Pi internals, and the surprisingly opinionated world of commercial display firmware. Along the way there were dead ends, a few Samsung displays that really did not want to be told what to do, and enough errno=64 errors to last a lifetime.
data.built-with#Built with: Raspberry Pi libCEC Flask Docker Ansible Ansible Semaphore Electron
data.cue#Cue: Cue runs on a Raspberry Pi and sends CEC commands to a display. It exposes a REST API for power on, standby, and input switching. Ansible and Semaphore handle deployment, so rolling it out to one display or twenty is the same amount of work.
data.director#Director:
Director is the desktop companion to Cue. It’s an Electron app that runs on any machine on the local network and gives you a clean interface for sending commands to one display or all of them at once. Configure it with a simple YAML file, point it at your Pis, and you’ve got a control surface that works on any OS without installing anything else.
For anyone who has ever handed an IR remote to someone and watched them aim it at the wrong thing, Director is the alternative.

data: Welcome to the Cue and Director documentation!
data.how-it-works#How it works:
When a command is received at the /command endpoint, Cue’s Python application reads your config.yml and executes the appropriate CEC sequence against the connected display. The persistent cec-client connection means commands get through even after a display enters deep sleep — something one-shot CEC tools can’t reliably do.
Director talks to those endpoints directly over the local network, fanning commands out to all configured displays in parallel when needed.
data.the-core-idea#The core idea:
A Raspberry Pi sits connected to a display over HDMI, maintains a persistent CEC connection, and waits for a command. When one arrives via the REST API, Cue handles the full sequence — power on, input switching, standby — in the right order, with the right timing. The entire flow runs inside a Docker container on the Pi, deployed and managed by an Ansible playbook.
For managing deployments across many devices, Cue integrates with Ansible Semaphore, giving you a UI to handle inventory, variables, and job runs without touching a terminal.
data.what-is-cue#What is Cue?: Cue is a lightweight display control service that sends CEC commands to HDMI-connected TVs from a Raspberry Pi. It can be deployed at scale across multiple devices using Ansible and Docker.
data.what-is-director#What is Director?: Director is the desktop companion to Cue. It’s a lightweight Electron app that runs on any machine on your local network and gives you a simple interface for sending commands to one display or all of them at once. Configure it with a YAML file, point it at your Pis, and you have a control surface that works on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
data.what-youll-need#What you\u0026rsquo;ll n: A Raspberry Pi (any model with an HDMI port) A display with HDMI-CEC support (look for Anynet+, BRAVIA Sync, SimpLink, or EasyLink in your display settings) An Ansible control node or Semaphore instance A machine to run Director on (Windows, macOS, or Linux)
data.where-to-go-next#Where to go next:
If you’re setting up for the first time, head to Getting Started to walk through Pi setup and deployment.
If you’re already up and running and want to tune timing or configure inputs, jump to Configuration.
If you’re managing multiple Pis through Semaphore, the Semaphore section covers inventory and variable setup.
If you’re looking for the Director desktop app, head to Director.

data: Cue exposes a small REST API on each Pi. All requests require the X-API-Key header.
data.authentication#Authentication:
Every request must include the API key set in config.yml:
X-API-Key: your-api-key Requests with a missing or incorrect key return 401 Unauthorized.
data.get-health#\u003ccode\u003eGET /health\u:
Returns the current status of the Cue service and CEC bus.
Request
curl -H "X-API-Key: yourkey" http://:5000/health Response
{ "status": "ok", "tv_id": "your-tv-id", "cec_client": "running", "bus_ready": true, "phys_addr": "2000" } Field Description status Always ok if the API is reachable tv_id The friendly label set in config.yml cec_client running or stopped bus_ready true if the display is on the CEC bus, false if in deep sleep phys_addr The Pi’s physical CEC address. ffff indicates the display has dropped off the bus
data.notes#Notes: The on command bypasses the bus_ready check intentionally. The display must be woken even when it has dropped off the CEC bus entirely. Input switch commands (input_hdmi*) will fail with 503 if the display is in deep sleep, since switching inputs requires the display to already be on. Commands run in background threads. Sending multiple commands in quick succession may produce unexpected results — wait for one sequence to complete before sending the next.
data.post-command#\u003ccode\u003ePOST /comma:
Send a command to the display.
Request
curl -X POST http://:5000/command \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "X-API-Key: yourkey" \ -d '{"command": "on"}' Body
{ "command": "on" } Commands
Command Description on Power on the display, assert Pi as active source, switch to content input off Assert Pi as active source, wait, then send standby input_hdmi1 Switch to HDMI 1 input_hdmi2 Switch to HDMI 2 input_hdmi3 Switch to HDMI 3 input_hdmi4 Switch to HDMI 4 Response
{ "status": "ok", "command": "on" } The API returns immediately — commands execute asynchronously in the background. Use /health to check the resulting bus state.
data.status-codes#Status codes: Code Meaning 200 Command accepted 400 Missing or unknown command 401 Invalid or missing API key 415 Missing Content-Type: application/json header 503 CEC bus not ready (display in deep sleep). Note: the on command bypasses this check

data: Cue is configured through a config.yml file that lives alongside the Docker container on each Pi. The Ansible playbook generates this file from a Jinja2 template using variables defined in your Semaphore inventory and environment.
data.api_key#\u003ccode\u003eapi_key\u003c/co:
Type: string Default: changeme
Required on all API requests via the X-API-Key header. Requests with a missing or incorrect key are rejected with a 401 Unauthorized response.
Generate a secure key with:
openssl rand -hex 32 Set this as a secret in Semaphore rather than hardcoding it in your inventory. See Semaphore for details.
data.api_port#\u003ccode\u003eapi_port\u003c/:
Type: integer Default: 5000
The port the Cue REST API listens on. Update this if port 5000 conflicts with something else on your network, and make sure to update your firewall rules and Director config accordingly.
data.bus_wait_timeout#\u003ccode\u003ebus_wai:
Type: integer (seconds) Default: 15
How long the on sequence will wait for the CEC bus to become ready before sending the content input switch. If the display does not come online within this window, the input switch is sent anyway with a warning in the logs.
data.content_hdmi_port#\u003ccode\u003econten:
Type: integer Default: 1
The HDMI port the content source (laptop, media player, etc.) is connected to. The on command switches the display to this input after powering on.
data.full-example#Full example: tv_id: "ad-br-tv-l" api_key: "your-api-key" pi_hdmi_port: 2 content_hdmi_port: 1 api_port: 5000 on_delay: 1 input_delay: 3 off_delay: 2 bus_wait_timeout: 15
data.input_delay#\u003ccode\u003einput_delay\:
Type: integer (seconds) Default: 3
How long to wait after asserting the active source before switching to the content input. This gives the display time to register the wake before the input switch is sent.
data.notes#Notes: The config file is generated by Ansible at deploy time. Direct edits on the Pi will be overwritten on the next deployment. The file is written with 0600 permissions so only root can read it. All timing values may need tuning depending on your display model and how quickly it responds to CEC commands.
data.off_delay#\u003ccode\u003eoff_delay\u003:
Type: integer (seconds) Default: 2
How long to wait between asserting the Pi as the active source and sending the standby command. Some displays need a moment after an input change before they will accept a standby command.
data.on_delay#\u003ccode\u003eon_delay\u003c/:
Type: integer (seconds) Default: 1
How long to wait between sending the power on command and asserting the Pi as the active source. Increase this if the display is slow to respond after waking.
data.pi_hdmi_port#\u003ccode\u003epi_hdmi_por:
Type: integer Default: 2
The HDMI port the Pi is physically connected to on the display. Used internally to understand the Pi’s position on the CEC bus. Run echo "scan" | cec-client -s -d 1 to find the Pi’s physical address — the first digit corresponds to the port number.
data.tv_id#\u003ccode\u003etv_id\u003c/code\u:
Type: string Default: tv-unknown
A friendly label for this Pi and display. Appears in the /health endpoint response. Useful for identifying which Pi you are talking to when managing multiple devices.

data: Director is the desktop companion to Cue. It is an Electron app that runs on any machine on your local network and gives you a clean interface for sending commands to one display or all of them at once.
data.all-displays#All displays: The All On and All Off buttons at the top send the command to every display simultaneously.
data.config-reference#Config reference: Field Description location Friendly name shown in the app header api_key Must match the api_key set on each Cue Pi displays[].id Unique identifier, used internally displays[].name Friendly name shown on the display card displays[].host IP address of the Pi displays[].port Port the Cue API is listening on (default: 5000) displays[].inputs List of HDMI input numbers to show as buttons
data.configuration#Configuration:
Director reads from a config.yml file. On first launch, it uses the default config shipped with the app. Any changes made through the settings UI are saved to a user config file that persists across updates:
macOS — ~/Library/Application Support/director/config.yml Windows — %APPDATA%\director\config.yml Linux — ~/.config/director/config.yml
data.display-cards#Display cards: Each display gets a card showing its name, ID, host, and current status. On and Off buttons send the corresponding command to that display. HDMI input buttons appear for each input defined in the config.
data.example-config#Example config: location: "Building A - Board Room" api_key: "your-api-key" displays: - id: your-pi-1 name: "Left" host: 192.168.1.101 port: 5000 inputs: [1, 2] - id: your-pi-2 name: "Center" host: 192.168.1.102 port: 5000 inputs: [1, 2] - id: your-pi-3 name: "Right" host: 192.168.1.103 port: 5000 inputs: [1, 2]
data.installation#Installation:
Download the latest release for your platform from the Director releases page:
macOS — .dmg Windows — .exe Linux — .AppImage On macOS, if you see an “unidentified developer” warning, right-click the app and select Open to bypass it on first launch.
data.multiple-locations#Multiple locations: To use Director in a different location, install it on a machine at that location and configure it with the appropriate Pis. Each instance only knows about the displays in its own config — there is no central server.
data.settings#Settings:
Click the gear icon in the top right to open the settings panel. From there you can update the location name, API key, and display list without editing the config file directly. Changes are saved immediately on clicking Save.
The settings panel also has buttons to open the config file in your system text editor or open the folder containing it, if you prefer to edit it manually.
data.status-dots#Status dots:
Each card has a status dot indicating the current state of that Pi:
Color Meaning Green Online and CEC bus ready Amber Online but CEC bus not ready Red Offline or unreachable Status is refreshed automatically every 15 seconds. Click the refresh button to check immediately.

data: This page walks through setting up Cue on a Raspberry Pi for the first time.
data.deploy-cue#Deploy Cue:
Cue is deployed using the included Ansible playbook. From your Ansible control node or Semaphore instance:
Clone the Cue repository Set up your inventory with your Pi’s IP address and variables (see Configuration and Semaphore) Run the playbook: ansible-playbook deploy-cue.yml -i your-inventory.yml The playbook will install Docker, generate the config file, and start the Cue container on the Pi.
data.enable-cec-on-your-display#Enable CEC on:
Before anything else, make sure CEC is enabled on your display. The setting name varies by manufacturer but is usually found under:
Samsung — Menu → General → External Device Manager → Anynet+ (HDMI-CEC) LG — Settings → General → SIMPLINK (HDMI-CEC) Sony — Settings → External Inputs → Bravia Sync Settings Others — check your display’s manual for “HDMI-CEC” or one of the brand names above
data.next-steps#Next steps: Head to Configuration to understand all available config values Head to Semaphore to set up multi-Pi deployments Head to API to start sending commands Head to Director to install the desktop control app
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites:
Before you begin, make sure you have:
A Raspberry Pi with a full HDMI port A display with HDMI-CEC enabled (look for Anynet+, BRAVIA Sync, SimpLink, or EasyLink in your display’s settings — it is often off by default) An HDMI cable connecting the Pi to the display Raspberry Pi OS installed and SSH access configured Docker and Docker Compose installed on the Pi An Ansible control node or Semaphore instance
data.verify-cec-is-working#Verify CEC is work:
SSH into your Pi and run a quick scan to confirm the display is visible on the CEC bus:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y cec-utils echo "scan" | cec-client -s -d 1 You should see your display listed as a device with a physical address. If nothing shows up, double-check that CEC is enabled on the display and that your HDMI cable is fully seated.
data.verify-cue-is-running#Verify Cue is runn:
Once deployed, check that the container is up and the API is responding:
curl -H "X-API-Key: yourkey" http://:5000/health You should get back something like:
{ "status": "ok", "tv_id": "your-tv-id", "cec_client": "running", "bus_ready": true, "phys_addr": "2000" } If bus_ready is false, the display may be in standby or deep sleep. This is normal — the on command will still attempt to wake it.

data: Cue is designed to be deployed and managed through Ansible Semaphore, which gives you a UI for handling inventory, secrets, and job runs across multiple Pis without touching a terminal.
data.environment-secrets#Environment (secrets:
Create a new environment in Semaphore and add the following variables:
Variable Type Description cue_api_key Secret API key written to each Pi’s config. Use the same value across all Pis. Generate with openssl rand -hex 32 semaphore_ip Variable IP address of the Semaphore server, used to set firewall rules on each Pi Mark cue_api_key as a secret so it is encrypted at rest and never shown in logs.
data.inventory#Inventory:
Create a new inventory in Semaphore using the Static YAML type. Define one host per Pi:
all: hosts: your-pi-1: ansible_host: 192.168.1.101 ansible_user: pi tv_id: your-pi-1 pi_hdmi_port: 2 content_hdmi_port: 1 on_delay: 1 input_delay: 3 off_delay: 2 bus_wait_timeout: 15 your-pi-2: ansible_host: 192.168.1.102 ansible_user: pi tv_id: your-pi-2 pi_hdmi_port: 2 content_hdmi_port: 1 your-pi-3: ansible_host: 192.168.1.103 ansible_user: pi tv_id: your-pi-3 pi_hdmi_port: 2 content_hdmi_port: 1 Only ansible_host, ansible_user, and tv_id are required per host. All timing and port values fall back to defaults if not specified.
data.job-template#Job template:
Create a job template with the following settings:
Field Value Name Deploy Cue Playbook deploy-cue.yml Inventory your inventory Environment your environment Repository your Cue repository To deploy to all Pis at once, leave the host pattern as all. To target a specific Pi, set the host pattern to that host’s name (e.g. your-pi-1).
data.per-host-vs-global-variables#Per-host vs:
Variables defined in the inventory apply per host. Variables defined in the environment apply globally to all hosts in a run.
Use the inventory for things that differ between Pis — display IDs, HDMI port assignments, timing values. Use the environment for things shared across all Pis — the API key and Semaphore IP.
data.running-a-deployment#Running a deploymen:
Click Run on the job template. Semaphore will SSH into each Pi in the inventory, install dependencies, generate the config file, and start or restart the Cue container.
Subsequent deployments are safe to run at any time. The container is recreated on each run with --force-recreate, so config changes take effect immediately.
data.setup-overview#Setup overview: Add your repository to Semaphore Create an inventory with your Pi host definitions Create an environment with your secrets Create a job template pointing at deploy-cue.yml Run the job
